title: Cars: from go-kart to electric car
description: The forces that move and stop a car: engine, gearbox, traction, brakes, cornering, aerodynamics and batteries — up to the design of a Formula SAE car, with a vehicle dynamics simulator.

car-01-forcas.title: The forces on a car
car-01-forcas.theory:
# A car is a body under forces

Everything a car does — accelerate, brake, corner — is explained by **Newton's 2nd law**:

```
F net = m · a
```

The acceleration `a` (m/s²) is the net force `F` (newtons, N) divided by the mass `m` (kg). With the **same force**, a **lighter car accelerates more**.

## The four main forces

- **Traction force**: the engine turns the wheels and the tyre pushes the ground backwards; the ground pushes the car forwards.
- **Aerodynamic drag**: the air resists the motion. It grows with the **square** of the speed: `F_air = ½ · ρ · Cd · A · v²`.
- **Rolling resistance**: the tyre deforms as it rolls. It is roughly `Crr · m · g` (Crr ≈ 0.012 on a road tyre).
- **Weight** (`m · g`): pulls the car down and is balanced by the ground. It matters because tyre grip depends on it.

The net force is **traction − drag − rolling**. At the start drag is almost zero and the car accelerates hard; near top speed the traction barely beats the air.

## Units

- 100 km/h = 100 ÷ 3.6 = **27.8 m/s**.
- 1 kW = 1000 W; power = force × speed.

## The simulator

It integrates `F = m·a` in steps of 5 milliseconds. The engine has a realistic power curve, the gearbox shifts by itself and the tyres have a grip limit. In this lesson you only change **mass** and **power**.
car-01-forcas.task: Make the car go from **0 to 100 km/h in 8.5 s or less**. Try reducing the mass and increasing the power, and watch the speed graph.
car-01-forcas.safety: The experiments here are simulator-only. **Never** test acceleration, braking or cornering on public roads: it is a traffic offence and puts lives at risk. Real tests only on a closed track, with safety equipment and supervision.
hints: Less mass: the same force gives more acceleration (a = F/m).
More power helps, but the front tyres have a limit: try something like 1000 kg and 110 kW.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 8.5 s or less

questions.prompt: A **1000 kg** car receives a net force of **3000 N**. What is the acceleration?
Why does the car accelerate less and less as it gets faster?
options: Because the engine heats up and loses power
Because drag grows with the square of the speed and the long gears deliver less force at the wheel
Because the car's mass increases with speed
Because tyre friction disappears at high speed
questions.explanation: Drag (½·ρ·Cd·A·v²) grows a lot with speed, and in longer gears the force at the wheel is smaller. The net force shrinks, so the acceleration does too.

questions.prompt: With a constant acceleration of **4 m/s²**, how long does it take to go from 0 to 100 km/h (27.8 m/s)?

car-02-motor.title: Engine: torque, power and revs
car-02-motor.theory:
# Torque and power

The engine produces **torque** (`T`, in N·m): the "turning force" on the crankshaft. **Power** is torque times rotational speed:

```
P = T · ω        with  ω = rpm · 2π / 60   (rad/s)
```

Example: 200 N·m at 3000 rpm → ω = 314 rad/s → P = 62,800 W = **62.8 kW**.

## The engine curve

A combustion engine does not deliver the same torque at every rpm. In this simulator we use the classic approximation:

```
P(x) = Pmax · (x + x² − x³)     x = rpm / rpm at maximum power
```

This gives **maximum torque at half** the max-power rpm (1.25 · Pmax/ωpk) and a **redline** at 1.15 times that rpm. Above it the engine cuts out.

- **Torque** defines the "push" in each gear.
- **Power** defines how fast you can go: at **top speed** the engine power (minus losses, ~10%) is all spent against the air and rolling: `P = (F_air + F_roll) · v`.

## Old units

- 1 cv (metric horsepower) = 0.7355 kW; 1 hp = 0.7457 kW.
- A small family car has ~60–80 kW; a sports car, 200–400 kW.

## Play and observe

Increase the **power** and watch the top speed rise. Change the **max-power rpm**: for the same power, more rpm means **less torque**.
car-02-motor.task: Give the car a **top speed of at least 210 km/h** and **0–100 km/h in 9 s or less**.
hints: Top speed depends on power: drag requires P ∝ v³.
With about 110 kW the car exceeds 210 km/h.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 9 s or less

questions.prompt: An engine delivers **200 N·m at 3000 rpm**. What is the power, in kW?
A **120 cv** engine has how many kW? (1 cv = 0.7355 kW)
Why is it **power** (and not just torque) that defines the top speed?
options: Because torque does not reach the wheels
Because at top speed the engine power equals the power spent against the air and rolling (force × speed)
Because the gearbox turns power into mass
questions.explanation: Power = force × speed. At constant speed, all the power at the wheel goes into beating drag and rolling; the gearbox can multiply torque but does not create power.

car-03-cambio.title: Gearbox: multiplying the torque
car-03-cambio.theory:
# Why does a car have gears?

The engine only works well in a range of revs (here, up to 1.15 × the max-power rpm). The wheels, however, turn from 0 up to thousands of rpm. The **gearbox** is a set of gears that trades **speed for torque**.

```
Wheel torque = T_engine × i_gear × i_differential × efficiency
Wheel force  = Wheel torque / wheel radius
Speed        = (rpm · 2π / 60) · radius / (i_gear × i_differential)
```

- **Large ratio** (short gear, e.g. 1st = 3.5): lots of torque, little speed.
- **Small ratio** (long gear, e.g. 0.8): little torque, lots of speed.
- The **differential** multiplies all the gears (e.g. 4.0).

## Choosing the ratios

- 1st gear too short: the wheel spins or 1st runs out quickly.
- Last gear too short: the engine hits the cut-off before the air limits the car — **low top speed**.
- Few gears with big jumps: after each shift the revs drop a lot and the engine leaves its good range.

In the simulator the intermediate ratios follow a **geometric progression** between 1st and the last, and each shift takes 0.2 s without traction. The car has all-wheel drive so that the limit is the engine, not the tyre.
car-03-cambio.task: Choose the number of gears and the ratios to make **0–100 km/h in 8 s or less** without losing the **200 km/h top speed**.
hints: Increase 1st gear and the differential to accelerate harder.
More gears keep the engine near maximum power. Try 6 gears, 1st = 3.5, last = 0.8 and differential 3.6.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 8 s or less

questions.prompt: The engine delivers **150 N·m**. With 1st gear of **3.5** and differential of **4.0**, what is the wheel torque (no losses)?
With that 2100 N·m torque on a wheel of radius **0.30 m**, what is the force on the ground?
What happens if **all** the gears are too short (large ratios)?
options: The car is slower at everything
It accelerates hard, but the engine reaches the cut-off early and the top speed drops
The top speed increases a lot
questions.explanation: Large ratios multiply the torque, but make the engine spin faster for the same speed; in the last gear it hits the rev limit before drag limits the car.

car-04-tracao.title: Traction and weight transfer
car-04-tracao.theory:
# The tyre's limit

A tyre only transmits force up to a limit: **F_max = μ · N**, where μ is the friction coefficient (≈ 0.9 on dry asphalt, 1.5 on racing tyres) and N is the normal force (the weight resting on that tyre). Beyond that, the wheel **spins** — and a spinning tyre transmits **less** force (kinetic friction < static).

## Weight transfer

When the car accelerates, the weight "goes backwards"; when it brakes, it "goes forwards". The amount is:

```
ΔW = m · a · h / L
```

- `h` = height of the centre of gravity (CG), `L` = wheelbase.
- High CG or short wheelbase → more transfer.

## Which wheels pull?

- **Front (FWD)**: cheap and compact, but when accelerating the front gets **lighter** — it spins easily with a lot of power.
- **Rear (RWD)**: gains weight when accelerating; great for high power.
- **All-wheel (AWD)**: uses the weight on all four wheels: maximum acceleration ≈ μ · g.

In the simulator the driver floors it: if the engine force exceeds the tyre limit, it counts the **wheelspin** time and the tyre then transmits only 85% of the limit.
car-04-tracao.task: This car has **160 kW** and front-wheel drive: it spins a lot. Adjust the drive and the weight distribution to make **0–100 km/h in 6 s or less** and **spin for 2 s at most**.
hints: With front-wheel drive, the weight leaves the front when accelerating.
All-wheel drive uses all four wheels: try AWD.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 6 s or less

questions.prompt: A **1300 kg** car accelerating at **4 m/s²**, CG at **0.55 m** height and wheelbase of **2.6 m**. How much weight (in N) moves from the front to the rear?
Why do very powerful cars usually have **rear** or **all-wheel** drive?
options: Because the engine is closer to the wheels
Because when accelerating the weight goes backwards, increasing the grip of the rear wheels
Because the rear wheels are bigger
Because front-wheel drive uses more fuel
questions.explanation: Weight transfer increases the normal force at the rear; since F_max = μ·N, the rear wheels can take more force.

questions.prompt: With all-wheel drive and μ = 0.9, what is the greatest possible acceleration (ignoring the air)?
questions.explanation: With all the weight on the driven wheels: a = μ·g = 0.9 × 9.81 ≈ 8.83 m/s².

car-05-frenagem.title: Braking, ABS and reaction time
car-05-frenagem.theory:
# Stopping is physics too

The total stopping distance has two parts:

```
Reaction distance = v · t_reaction
Braking distance ≈ v² / (2 · a)
```

- At 100 km/h (27.8 m/s), each **1 s** of reaction is **27.8 m** before you touch the brake.
- Braking depends on **v²**: double the speed gives **four times** the distance.
- The best possible is `a = μ · g`: with μ = 0.9 → 8.8 m/s² → **44 m** from 100 km/h.

## Brake balance and lock-up

When braking, the weight goes to the **front** (ΔW = m·a·h/L). That is why the front brakes do 65–80% of the work (the **balance**). If a wheel asks for more force than μ·N, it **locks**:

- **Front** wheels locked: the car does not obey the steering wheel (it goes straight).
- **Rear** wheels locked: the rear slides and the car **spins** — very dangerous.
- A locked tyre drags with only ~75% of the friction: the distance increases.

## ABS

**ABS** (anti-lock braking system) measures the speed of each wheel and eases the brake when it starts to lock, keeping the tyre near maximum friction (in the simulator, 95% of the limit) and the car controllable.
car-05-frenagem.task: At 100 km/h, with a distracted driver (1.5 s reaction), the car stops too far away. Make the **braking at most 50 m**, the **total stop at most 80 m** and **without locking the rear wheels**.
car-05-frenagem.safety: Real braking distances depend on tyres, road surface and attention. **Never** use your phone while driving: 2 seconds looking at the screen at 100 km/h is 55 m travelled blind. Do not do braking tests on public roads.
hints: More brake force shortens the braking, but may lock the wheels. ABS prevents the lock-up.
A 1.5 s reaction costs 42 m! An attentive driver reacts in about 1 s. Try ABS on, 14 kN and 1 s reaction.

questions.prompt: At **100 km/h**, how many metres does the car travel during **1 s** of reaction?
questions.explanation: 100 km/h = 27.8 m/s; in 1 s the car travels 27.8 m without braking.

questions.prompt: At **72 km/h** (20 m/s), with μ = 0.8, what is the shortest possible braking distance?
If the speed doubles, the braking distance…
questions.explanation: The distance depends on v²: (2v)² = 4v². That is why small excesses in speed increase the distance a lot.

car-06-curvas.title: Corners, tyres and rollover
car-06-curvas.theory:
# The force that makes the turn

To go in a circle, the car needs a force towards the **centre** of the curve (centripetal force):

```
F = m · v² / r        lateral acceleration = v² / r
```

The **tyres** provide this force, up to the limit `μ · m · g`. Equating:

```
v_max = √(μ · g · r)
```

- A 50 m corner with μ = 0.9 → v_max = 21 m/s = **76 km/h**.
- Doubling μ does **not** double the speed: it grows with the **root**.
- Beyond the limit: the car **understeers** and widens its path.

Lateral acceleration is usually given in **g**: 1 g = 9.81 m/s². Road cars reach ~0.9 g; race cars, 1.5 g or more.

## Rollover

In a corner, weight also transfers to the **outside** wheels. If the lateral acceleration exceeds

```
a_rollover = g · track / (2 · h_CG)
```

the inside wheels lift and the car **rolls over before it slides**. That is why SUVs (high CG) roll over more and race cars are low and wide.

## Downforce

Wings and the car's underbody push the car **against the ground** (`½·ρ·ClA·v²`). More normal force → more grip, without more mass. But it only shows up at **high speed**.
car-06-curvas.task: The corner has a **radius of 50 m** and you must take it at **90 km/h** (at least **1.2 g** of lateral acceleration) **without leaving the track** and **without risk of rolling over**.
hints: v_max = √(μ·g·r): for 90 km/h (25 m/s) on 50 m you need μ ≥ 1.28.
Grippier tyres (μ = 1.3) solve it; if you raise μ too much, the car risks rolling over — lower the CG.
goals: Takes the corner without leaving the track

questions.prompt: What is the maximum speed in a corner of **100 m** radius with μ = **0.8**?
A utility vehicle has a track width of **1.5 m** and CG at **0.75 m**. From how many g does it tend to roll over?
questions.explanation: a/g = track / (2·h) = 1.5 / 1.5 = 1.0 g. If the tyres can take more than that, it rolls over before it slides.

questions.prompt: Why are race cars low and wide?
options: A low CG and wide track raise the rollover limit and reduce weight transfer
questions.explanation: The rollover limit is track/(2h): low and wide raises that limit and reduces the lateral weight transfer, which worsens the total grip.

car-07-aerodinamica.title: Aerodynamics and fuel consumption
car-07-aerodinamica.theory:
# The air is the biggest enemy on the road

The drag force is:

```
F_air = ½ · ρ · Cd · A · v²
```

- `ρ` ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ (air density), `A` = frontal area (m²), `Cd` = drag coefficient (the car's shape).
- Typical Cd: truck 0.6–0.8; small family car 0.33; efficient car 0.22–0.26.

The **power** to beat the air is force × speed:

```
P_air = ½ · ρ · Cd · A · v³
```

With **v³**, double the speed requires **8 times** the power. From ~60 km/h on, the air spends more than rolling.

## From the engine to the tank

- Power at the wheel = (F_air + F_rolling) · v.
- The gearbox loses ~10%; a petrol engine turns only **20–35%** of the fuel energy into work (the rest becomes heat).
- 1 litre of petrol ≈ **8.9 kWh**.

```
Consumption (L/100 km) = Energy per km / 8.9 kWh × 100
```

Reducing **Cd·A** also raises the top speed, because there is power left over.
car-07-aerodinamica.task: On the highway, at **120 km/h**, make the car use **at most 7 L/100 km** and reach **205 km/h** top speed — by improving the aerodynamics.
hints: Drag depends on Cd × A. Reduce both.
A car with Cd 0.26 and an area of 1.9 m² reaches both goals.

questions.prompt: What is the drag force on a car with Cd = **0.30**, A = **2.2 m²**, at **30 m/s** (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³)?
What power (in kW) is spent just against that drag at 30 m/s?
If the speed doubles, the power spent against the air…
questions.explanation: The force grows with v² and the power with v³: 2³ = 8.

car-08-suspensao.title: Suspension: springs, dampers and handling
car-08-suspensao.theory:
# What is the suspension for?

The suspension keeps the **tyres on the ground** (grip) and the **car stable and comfortable**. The two basic elements:

- **Spring**: stores energy and supports the weight. Force = `k · x` (k = stiffness, N/m; x = deflection).
- **Damper**: turns the motion into heat and **stops the oscillation**. Without it the car would keep bouncing like a ball.

## The "quarter car" model

Each wheel supports ~1/4 of the mass. Spring + mass form an oscillator with natural frequency:

```
f = (1 / 2π) · √(k / m)
```

- Passenger cars: **1.0–1.5 Hz** (soft, comfortable).
- Race cars: **2–5 Hz** (hard, little roll).

The static deflection (how much the spring sinks when stationary) is `x = m·g / k`.

## Behaviour in corners

- **Understeer** (front slides out): the front loses grip first; the car takes a wider turn than the steering asks for.
- **Oversteer** (rear slides out): the rear slides; the car turns more than requested.
- **Anti-roll bar**: links the wheels of the same axle and reduces the body **roll**; stiffening the front bar increases understeer.
- **Camber**: the wheel's tilt seen from the front. A little negative camber keeps the tyre better planted in the corner.

## Common geometries

- **MacPherson**: simple and cheap (most small cars).
- **Double wishbone**: controls camber better; used in sports cars and Formula SAE.
- **Torsion beam**: rear of compact cars.

questions.prompt: A quarter car has **300 kg** and a spring of **30,000 N/m**. What is the natural frequency?
What is the main function of the **damper**?
options: Support the weight of the car
Dissipate energy and make the spring's oscillation stop quickly
questions.explanation: The spring supports the weight; the damper turns the motion energy into heat, preventing the car from continuing to oscillate.

questions.prompt: In a corner, the car widens its path even with the steering wheel turned: the front wheels lost grip first. This is…
questions.explanation: Understeer (front slides out) is when the front axle reaches its limit before the rear.

questions.prompt: With the same spring (30,000 N/m) and 300 kg, how much does the spring sink when stationary?
What does the **anti-roll bar** do?
options: Absorbs bumps on one wheel only
questions.explanation: It twists when one side goes up and the other down, resisting roll; that is why it keeps the car "flatter" in corners.

car-09-eletrico.title: Electric car: energy and range
car-09-eletrico.theory:
# Electric: fewer parts, different physics

An electric motor delivers **maximum torque from 0 rpm** and keeps **constant power** at high revs. That is why the electric car uses **a single gear** (a reduction of ~9:1) and pulls away very strongly.

```
Wheel force = min( T_motor · reduction / radius ,  P_motor / v ) × 0.95
```

## Energy and range

- Battery: capacity in **kWh** (energy). An average car has 40–80 kWh.
- Typical consumption: **13–20 kWh/100 km**.
- Battery-to-wheel efficiency is high: **85–92%** (petrol: 20–35%).

```
Range (km) = Capacity (kWh) / Consumption (kWh/100 km) × 100
```

## The weight dilemma

Batteries are heavy: current packs store ~**160 Wh/kg**. A 75 kWh battery weighs ~470 kg! More battery = more range, but also more mass (worse acceleration and more rolling resistance). The simulator adds the battery mass to the car.

## Regenerative braking

When braking, the motor becomes a **generator** and returns part of the energy to the battery — which is why electric cars use little in city traffic (the simulator only measures the highway at constant speed, without regeneration).
car-09-eletrico.task: Design an electric car with a **range of at least 400 km at 100 km/h** that does **0–100 km/h in 7 s or less**.
car-09-eletrico.safety: Electric car batteries work at **400 to 800 V** direct current: lethal voltage. Only trained technicians with insulated equipment work on the high-voltage system (orange cables). Damaged lithium batteries can catch fire hours later; never puncture or heat cells.
hints: A bigger battery gives range, but is heavy: compensate with efficiency and aerodynamics.
Try 75 kWh, 90% efficiency, a 150 kW and 350 N·m motor with all-wheel drive.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 7 s or less

questions.prompt: A car with a **60 kWh** battery uses **15 kWh/100 km**. What is the range?
How much does a **60 kWh** pack weigh at **160 Wh/kg**?
Why do electric cars usually use **less** in the city than on the highway (the opposite of petrol cars)?
options: Because in the city the speed is low (little drag) and regenerative braking recovers energy
Because the electric motor has an automatic gearbox
Because city air is less dense
questions.explanation: Drag grows with v², and when braking the motor works as a generator and recharges the battery.

car-10-projeto-fsae.title: Project: lap time of a Formula SAE car
car-10-projeto-fsae.theory:
# Engineering is compromise

In **Formula SAE**, university teams design and build a small race car (~300 kg with driver, ~60 kW with an intake restrictor). What matters is the **lap time**, and almost every decision improves one thing and worsens another.

## The lap model

Our track is an oval: two 75 m straights and two 180° corners with a 15 m radius. The simulator does what a track engineer does in a spreadsheet ("point-mass simulation"):

- **Corners** at the tyre limit: `v = √(μ·g·r)`, or, with downforce,

```
m·v²/r = μ·(m·g + ½·ρ·ClA·v²)   →   v² = μ·m·g / (m/r − μ·ρ·ClA/2)
```

- **Straights**: maximum acceleration (engine, gears and traction) from the corner exit speed, and braking at the limit (`μ·(m·g + downforce)`) to reach the next corner at the right speed.
- Time = sum of distance / speed in each section.

## The design levers

- **Downforce (ClA)**: faster corners, shorter braking — but the wing has drag (here ClA/3), which **steals speed on the straight**.
- **Mass**: less mass helps everything (corner, straight and braking), but the rules and safety impose a minimum.
- **Gear ratios**: on a tight layout, shorter gears keep the engine in its power band.

On tracks with long straights, the optimum is **less wing**; on tight tracks (like FSAE), **more wing** usually wins. Test both limits and watch the speed graph along the lap.
car-10-projeto-fsae.task: Do a lap in **12.5 s at most** while keeping at least **100 km/h at the end of the straight** (the car must not become a "brick" with too much wing).
hints: Add downforce little by little and watch the lap time and the top speed on the straight.
Combine ClA ≈ 4, differential 4.5 and a mass of 280 kg.
goals: Speed at the end of the straight ≥ 100 km/h

questions.prompt: With no downforce, μ = **1.4** and a radius of **15 m**, what is the maximum corner speed?
With m = **300 kg**, μ = **1.5**, r = **15 m**, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³ and ClA = **3 m²**, what is the maximum corner speed?
On a track with **very long straights** and few corners, what tends to give the best time?
options: Little wing: drag costs more on the straights than the extra grip gains in the corners
questions.explanation: The wing's gain shows up in the corners; the cost (drag) shows up on every straight. With long straights, the cost dominates (in the same model, with 250 m straights, the best ClA drops to about 1).

car-11-velocidade-maxima.title: Top speed: power against the air and the right gear
car-11-velocidade-maxima.theory:
# What limits top speed

At top speed the engine's force at the wheels equals the sum of the resistances. At high speed **aerodynamic drag** is in charge, and the power to overcome it grows with the **cube** of the speed:

```
P_air = ½ × ρ × Cd × A × v³
```

At 200 km/h (55.6 m/s), a car with Cd = 0.30 and A = 2.2 m² spends ~**68 kW** against the air alone. That's why **doubling the power** raises top speed by only about **26%** (∛2 ≈ 1.26).

## Two ways not to get there

1. **Too little power or too much drag**: the engine lacks the force to push faster. Fix: less Cd × A (shape, frontal area) or more power.
2. **Gearing too short**: the engine hits the **rev limit** (rev limiter) before the power runs out. The speed at the limit is:

```
v = max_rpm × 2π/60 × wheel_radius / (gear ratio × final drive)
```

With 6670 rpm, top gear 0.85, final drive 5.0 and a 0.30 m wheel: v ≈ 49.3 m/s = **177 km/h**, even if the engine had power for more.

## The sweet spot

Top speed is best when the top gear brings the engine close to its **peak-power rpm** exactly at the speed where power equals the resistances. Gearing too long also loses: the engine "bogs down", below peak-power rpm.

## In this lab

A 1300 kg car with **100 kW** (peak power at 5800 rpm, limiter at 6670 rpm). You can't touch the engine: only the **aerodynamics** and the **ratios**.
car-11-velocidade-maxima.task: The car won't go past 178 km/h. Without touching the engine, make it reach **220 km/h** by adjusting the **final drive**, the **top gear**, the **Cd** and the **frontal area**.
hints: With a 5.0 final drive the engine hits the limiter. Lengthen the gearing (final drive near 3.6) and see the new limit.
Gearing alone gets you to ~208 km/h. The rest comes from the air: a Cd of 0.28 and an area of 2.0 m² make the difference.
goals: Top speed of at least 220 km/h

questions.prompt: How much power goes into the air alone at **200 km/h**, with Cd = **0.30**, A = **2.2 m²** and ρ = 1.2 kg/m³?
The engine cuts out at **6670 rpm**. With top gear **0.85**, final drive **5.0** and a **0.30 m** wheel radius, what is the speed at the limiter?
If only the air mattered, doubling the power would raise top speed by…

car-12-escalonamento.title: Gear spacing: speed per rpm and rev drops
car-12-escalonamento.theory:
# Each gear is a "band" of speeds

With wheel radius r, gear ratio i and final drive d, the speed at an engine speed n (rpm) is:

```
v = n × 2π/60 × r / (i × d)
```

A practical measure is the **speed per 1000 rpm**: with top gear 0.80, final drive 3.6 and a 0.30 m wheel, that's ~**39.3 km/h per 1000 rpm** — at 6000 rpm, ~236 km/h.

## Geometric progression

Gears usually follow a **geometric progression**: each one is the previous one times the same factor q:

```
q = (i_top / i_1st)^(1 / (N − 1))
```

With 1st = 3.5, top = 0.8 and 6 gears: q = (0.8/3.5)^(1/5) ≈ **0.744**.

## The rev drop on a shift

During a shift the car's speed stays the same, so the engine speed drops by the same ratio as the gears:

```
n_after = n_before × (i_next / i_current) = n_before × q
```

Shifting at 6000 rpm with q = 0.744, the engine drops to ~**4466 rpm**. Ideally this drop keeps the engine in its **high-power** band. More gears → q closer to 1 → smaller drops → better acceleration (hence 8- to 10-speed gearboxes and the CVT, which varies the ratio continuously).

## Real spacing

In practice the high gears are **closer together** than the low ones ("progressive" spacing): at high speed drag demands keeping the engine always near peak power.

questions.prompt: At **6000 rpm**, with top gear **0.8**, final drive **3.6** and a **0.30 m** wheel, what is the speed?
In that same gear, how many km/h does the car go per **1000 rpm**?
A **6-speed** gearbox goes from **3.5** (1st) to **0.8** (6th) in geometric progression. What is the factor q between neighbouring gears?
Shifting at **6000 rpm** in this gearbox, what rpm does the engine drop to?
questions.explanation: 6000 × 0.744 ≈ 4466 rpm (the car's speed doesn't change during the shift).

questions.prompt: Why do gearboxes with **more gears** accelerate better?
options: Because the engine becomes more powerful
Because the rev drops are smaller and the engine stays longer near peak power
questions.explanation: With q closer to 1, each shift drops the revs less: the average power at the wheels goes up.

car-13-balanco-freio.title: Brake balance: the perfect stop without ABS
car-13-balanco-freio.theory:
# The weight moves forward

When braking with deceleration a, part of the weight moves from the rear wheels to the front ones (**load transfer**):

```
N_front = m g × (front fraction) + m a × h / L
```

(h: CG height; L: wheelbase). A 1300 kg car with 60% of the weight on the front, CG at 0.55 m and a 2.6 m wheelbase, braking at 0.8 g, has ~**9810 N** on the front — **77%** of the weight.

## Each axle has its limit

Each axle can only brake up to μ × N. If an axle gets more brake force than that, the wheel **locks**:

- **Front locked**: the car won't steer (goes straight).
- **Rear locked**: the car tends to **spin** — much more dangerous. That's why brake force always goes more to the front.

## Ideal balance

The shortest possible stop happens when **both axles reach their limit together**: the fraction of brake force on the front should equal the fraction of load on the front **during braking**:

```
ideal balance = N_front / (m g)
```

Since the transfer depends on the deceleration, the ideal balance changes with grip; cars use **proportioning valves** and today **electronic brake-force distribution** (EBD) together with ABS.

## Without ABS

Without ABS, too much brake force locks the wheels (a locked tyre has only ~75% of the friction). The trick is to brake **as hard as possible without locking**, with the right balance.

## In this lab

A 1300 kg car, 60% of the weight on the front, μ = 0.9, braking from 100 km/h **without ABS**.
car-13-balanco-freio.task: Without ABS, stop the car from 100 km/h within **47 m** of braking **without locking either axle**. Adjust the **brake force** and the **balance** (front brake share).
car-13-balanco-freio.safety:
- Real brake testing only on a **closed track**, with a trained driver and an inspected car. On the street, keep your distance and brake early.
- Locking the rear wheels at high speed can make the car **spin**.
hints: With 60% of the brake on the front, the rear axle locks early: in hard braking, the front carries ~77% of the weight.
Set the balance near 78% and the force between 10 and 11 kN.

questions.prompt: A **1300 kg** car, **60%** of the weight on the front, CG at **0.55 m**, **2.6 m** wheelbase, braking at **0.8 g**. How much load is on the front axle? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
What is the ideal brake balance (percentage on the front) for that 0.8 g stop?
Why is it more dangerous to lock the **rear** wheels than the front ones?
options: Because the rear slides out and the car tends to spin
Because the rear brakes get hotter
questions.explanation: With the front locked the car goes straight (it just can't steer); with the rear locked, any small deviation becomes a spin.

car-14-energia-freios.title: Where braking energy goes: heat, fade and regeneration
car-14-energia-freios.theory:
# Braking turns motion into heat

A 1500 kg car at 100 km/h has kinetic energy:

```
E = ½ × m × v² = ½ × 1500 × 27.8² ≈ 579 kJ
```

In a stop, almost all of it becomes **heat in the discs and pads**, within a few seconds.

## Braking power

At the start of hard braking, the power is **m × a × v**: at 0.8 g and 100 km/h, that's ~**327 kW** — more than twice the engine power of an ordinary car!

## How hot the disc gets

If 70% of the energy goes to the **two front discs** of 8 kg of steel (specific heat 460 J/(kg·K)):

```
ΔT = E_front / (m_discs × c) = 0.7 × 579 000 / (16 × 460) ≈ 55 °C
```

A single stop is little; several in a row (mountain descent, track) add heat faster than the air can remove it.

## Fade

Above a certain temperature the pad friction **drops** (fade) and the brake fluid may **boil** (bubbles → "spongy" pedal). Remedies: bigger, ventilated discs, high-temperature pads, air ducts, high-boiling-point fluid — and, going downhill, **engine braking** (lower gear).

## Regenerative braking

Electric and hybrid cars use the motor as a **generator**: part of the energy goes back to the battery (60–70% in gentle braking). 60% of 579 kJ is ~**0.096 kWh** — little per stop, but in the city there are hundreds a day. In hard stops the friction brakes are still needed.

questions.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a **1500 kg** car at **100 km/h**? Answer in kJ.
What is the braking power at the **start** of a **0.8 g** stop of this car (1500 kg, 100 km/h)? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
70% of that energy goes to **two 8 kg** steel discs (c = 460 J/(kg·K)). How much do they heat up in one stop?
An EV recovers **60%** of that energy when braking. How many kWh go back to the battery? (1 kWh = 3.6 MJ)
On a long mountain descent, what helps most to avoid **brake fade**?
options: Coasting in neutral to save fuel
Using a lower gear (engine braking) and braking hard only when needed
Inflating the tyres to a higher pressure
questions.explanation: Engine braking removes energy without heating the discs; braking hard and briefly gives them time to cool between stops.

car-15-downforce.title: Downforce: grip from the air (and its price)
car-15-downforce.theory:
# Pushing the car onto the ground

An inverted wing (or a well-shaped floor) creates **downforce**, a downward force that grows with the square of the speed:

```
F_down = ½ × ρ × ClA × v²
```

(ClA: lift coefficient × area, in m²). At 30 m/s, ClA = 3 m² gives ½ × 1.2 × 3 × 900 = **1620 N** — the weight of 165 kg, with no mass at all!

## More grip in the corner

The tyre holds μ × (weight + downforce). In the corner, the centripetal force m v²/r must fit within that:

```
m v² / r = μ × (m g + ½ ρ ClA v²)
v = √(μ m g / (m/r − μ ½ ρ ClA))
```

Without a wing, a 700 kg car with μ = 1.3 on a 50 m corner can do at most √(μ g r) ≈ 25.3 m/s (91 km/h). With ClA = 3.2 m², ~27.9 m/s (100 km/h).

## The price: drag

Every wing that makes downforce also makes **drag** (here, ~1/3 of ClA becomes drag area). On the straight, it **steals top speed**. Twisty tracks are worth more wing; tracks with long straights, less (lesson 19).

## Why doesn't it roll over?

A car rolls over before sliding when μ > track / (2 × CG height). Low, wide race cars (1.5 m track, CG at 0.35 m: limit 2.1 g) slide long before they roll.

## In this lab

A 700 kg car, μ = 1.3, 50 m radius corner at **100 km/h**, 80 kW engine.
car-15-downforce.task: Make the car take the corner at 100 km/h (**corner OK**) with no rollover risk, but don't overdo the wing: **top speed** on the straight must stay **above 140 km/h**.
hints: Without a wing the limit is ~91 km/h. Raise ClA little by little and see when the corner works.
The corner works from ClA ≈ 3.2; above ~3.6 the top speed drops below 140 km/h.
goals: Top speed of at least 140 km/h

questions.prompt: What is the downforce of a wing with ClA = **3 m²** at **30 m/s** (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³)?
Without a wing, what is the top speed on a **50 m** corner with μ = **1.3**? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
With ClA = **3.2 m²**, m = **700 kg**, μ = 1.3, r = 50 m and ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, what is the top corner speed? (v = √(μmg / (m/r − μ·½·ρ·ClA)))

car-16-suspensao-avancada.title: Suspension in depth: damping, motion ratio and frequencies
car-16-suspensao-avancada.theory:
# The car as mass–spring–damper

Each corner of the car is a mass (m) on a spring (k) and a damper (c). In lesson 8 we saw the natural frequency f = √(k/m) / 2π. Now, the other two numbers every suspension engineer uses.

## Damping ratio ζ

```
ζ = c / (2 × √(k × m))
```

- ζ < 1: **underdamped** — bounces a few times before stopping.
- ζ = 1: **critical** — returns fastest without overshooting.
- ζ > 1: **overdamped** — harsh, returns slowly.

Passenger cars use ζ ≈ 0.2–0.4 (comfort); race cars, 0.5–0.8 (control).

## Motion ratio

The spring is rarely right above the wheel: it moves **less** than the wheel. If the spring moves MR times the wheel travel, the stiffness **felt at the wheel** is:

```
k_wheel = k_spring × MR²
```

With MR = 0.7, a 40 000 N/m spring becomes 19 600 N/m at the wheel — the **square** of the ratio, because both force and displacement change.

## Typical frequencies

- Luxury cars: ~1.0–1.2 Hz (soft).
- Sports cars: 1.5–2.0 Hz.
- Formula cars with lots of downforce: 3–5 Hz (very stiff, so the floor doesn't hit the ground).

The rear is usually ~10% stiffer than the front, so the car doesn't "pitch" over bumps.

## Roll

In a corner, the lateral load transfer is m × a_y × h / track. **Anti-roll bars** split that transfer between front and rear: more stiffness at the front → more understeer; more at the rear → more oversteer.

questions.prompt: A corner of the car has m = **300 kg**, k = **30 000 N/m** and damper c = **3000 N·s/m**. What is the damping ratio ζ?
A **40 000 N/m** spring is mounted with a motion ratio of **0.7**. What stiffness is felt at the wheel?
With that wheel rate (19 600 N/m) and **250 kg** on the corner, what is the natural frequency?
With ζ much **lower** than recommended (weak/worn damper), the car…
options: Bounces several times after each bump and loses grip
questions.explanation: Too little damping lets the oscillation go on; the tyre alternates between high and low load and the car "floats".

questions.prompt: Stiffening the **front** anti-roll bar tends to make the car…
options: More understeery (the front loses grip first)
More comfortable in a straight line
questions.explanation: More stiffness at the front puts more of the load transfer on the front axle; the outer front tyre saturates first.

car-17-ev-estrada.title: EV on the highway: battery, weight and aerodynamics
car-17-ev-estrada.theory:
# Why highway range is the EV's problem

In the city, an EV recovers energy when braking and barely uses any standing still. On the **highway**, at 110 km/h, almost all the energy goes into the **air** and **rolling**:

```
F = ½ ρ Cd A v² + Crr × m × g
P_wheel = F × v
consumption (kWh/100 km) = P_wheel / η / v × 100 km
```

A 2100 kg car with Cd = 0.23, A = 2.2 m² and Crr = 0.012 at 110 km/h: F ≈ 283 + 247 = **531 N**, P ≈ **16.2 kW**, and with η = 88% ≈ **16.8 kWh/100 km** (plus auxiliaries).

## The battery's vicious circle

More battery = more range, but the battery **weighs** (~160 Wh/kg at pack level: 80 kWh ≈ **500 kg**). More weight = more rolling resistance, more energy to accelerate, bigger brakes and suspension, worse acceleration. Range grows **less** than the battery.

## Where the cheap gain is

- **Cd × A**: at 110 km/h the air is more than half the force. Fairings, covered wheels, camera mirrors and a flat floor bring modern EVs to Cd ≈ 0.20–0.23.
- **Low-rolling-resistance tyres** (lower Crr).
- **Efficiency** of the inverter–motor–reduction gear chain (85–92%).

## Speed

Since air force grows with v², driving at 130 instead of 110 km/h raises consumption by ~25–30%. For EVs cruising speed matters more than for combustion cars, because the battery stores little energy compared with a fuel tank.

## In this lab

Mass without battery 1600 kg, 150 kW motor with 350 N·m, rear-wheel drive, battery-to-wheel efficiency 88%, cruise at **110 km/h**.
car-17-ev-estrada.task: Design the EV for the highway: **range ≥ 450 km** at 110 km/h, **consumption ≤ 18 kWh/100 km**, **0–100 km/h within 8.7 s** and **total mass ≤ 2150 kg**. Choose the **battery**, the **Cd** and the **frontal area**.
hints: Just growing the battery won't do: with 100 kWh the car goes over 2200 kg and still uses 21 kWh/100 km.
Start with the aerodynamics (Cd 0.23, area 2.2 m²) and then set the battery near 80 kWh.
goals: Range of at least 450 km at 110 km/h

questions.prompt: A **2100 kg** car, Cd = **0.23**, A = **2.2 m²**, Crr = **0.012**, at **110 km/h** (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²). What is the power at the wheels?
With **88%** battery-to-wheel efficiency, how much does this car use per 100 km (not counting auxiliaries)?
How much does an **80 kWh** pack at **160 Wh/kg** weigh?

car-18-motor-termico.title: Combustion engine: thermal efficiency, BSFC and emissions
car-18-motor-termico.theory:
# How much of the fuel becomes motion

A petrol engine turns heat into work following (in idealised form) the **Otto cycle**. Its theoretical efficiency depends only on the **compression ratio** r:

```
η_Otto = 1 − r^(1 − γ)      (γ ≈ 1.4 for air)
```

With r = 10: η = 1 − 10^(−0.4) ≈ **60%**. Real engines reach **25–40%**: friction, heat lost through the walls, pumping (a closed throttle) and combustion that isn't instantaneous. The compression ratio is limited by **knock** (detonation); diesel engines compress more (15–20) and are more efficient.

## BSFC: the dyno number

In practice one measures the **specific fuel consumption** (BSFC): grams of fuel per kWh delivered at the shaft. The efficiency follows directly:

```
η = 3.6 × 10⁶ / (BSFC [kg/kWh] × LHV [J/kg])
```

With BSFC = 250 g/kWh and petrol with a heating value of 43 MJ/kg: η ≈ **33.5%**. The best passenger-car engines reach ~200 g/kWh (~41%).

## From engine to road

If a car needs **15 kW** at the wheels at 100 km/h (15 kWh every 100 km) and the engine + transmission is 30% efficient, with petrol at 8.9 kWh/L:

```
consumption = 15 / (0.30 × 8.9) ≈ 5.6 L/100 km
```

## CO₂

Burning 1 L of petrol releases ~**2.3 kg of CO₂** (the fuel's carbon becomes CO₂). A car using 6 L/100 km emits ~138 g of CO₂ per km — and the only way to reduce that is to **burn less fuel** (or switch energy source).

questions.prompt: What is the theoretical Otto-cycle efficiency with a compression ratio of **10** (γ = 1.4)?
An engine has a BSFC of **250 g/kWh** burning petrol at **43 MJ/kg**. What is its real efficiency?
A car needs **15 kW** at the wheels at 100 km/h. With a total efficiency of **30%** and petrol at **8.9 kWh/L**, how much does it use?
questions.explanation: Over 100 km (1 h) the wheels need 15 kWh. Fuel = 15 / 0.30 = 50 kWh = 50 / 8.9 ≈ 5.6 L.

questions.prompt: Each litre of petrol burned releases **2.3 kg** of CO₂. How much CO₂ per km does a car using **6 L/100 km** emit?
What prevents simply raising a petrol engine's compression ratio a lot?
questions.explanation: Compression heats the mixture; above a certain point it explodes on its own, violently, and damages the engine. Diesel avoids this by injecting the fuel only at the end of compression.

car-19-acerto-asa.title: Wing setup: fast track, less wing
car-19-acerto-asa.theory:
# Each track needs its own setup

In lesson 10 the Formula SAE car ran on a **twisty** track (tight corners, short straights), and more downforce always helped. On a **fast** track — long straights and large-radius corners — the maths changes:

- In the **corners**, downforce raises the speed, and a fast corner has a lot of speed to gain.
- On the **straights**, the wing's drag limits top speed. When top speed drops **below the speed possible in the corner**, the extra wing is useless: the car already enters the corner at the engine's limit.

## Lap time

```
time ≈ Σ (length of each section / average speed in that section)
```

A 400 m straight at an average of 130 km/h takes ~11 s; a half-lap of radius 60 m is π × 60 ≈ 188 m long.

## The optimal setup

There is a wing level at which the corner speed **almost reaches** the straight's top speed. With less wing, you lose in the corners; with more, you lose on the straights (and in the corners themselves, which become limited by top speed). Race teams bring **several wings** and pick one per track — Monza (straights) uses very thin wings; Monaco (slow corners), the biggest.

## In this lab

The same car as in lesson 10 (300 kg, 60 kW), now on an oval with **400 m** straights and **60 m** radius corners. It arrived with the twisty-track wing (ClA = 4).
car-19-acerto-asa.task: With the twisty-track wing the car laps in ~36 s. Adjust the **wing (ClA)** and the **ratios** to lap in **33.2 s or less**.
hints: Compare the corner speed with the top speed: with ClA = 4 they are equal — there's too much wing.
Try ClA in steps of 1. The best time is near 2.

questions.prompt: How long does the car take on a **400 m** straight at an average of **130 km/h**?
How long is a **half-turn** (180°) corner with a **60 m** radius?
With ClA = 4 on this track, why doesn't the extra wing help in the corners anymore?
options: Because drag pulled top speed below what the corner could take
Because downforce doesn't work in big corners
Because the car becomes too heavy
questions.explanation: If the engine only gets the car to 118 km/h, it doesn't matter that the corner could take more: the corner speed is capped by top speed.

car-20-projeto-esportivo.title: Final project: a fast, safe and economical sports car
car-20-projeto-esportivo.theory:
# A car is a set of compromises

Car engineers never optimise one thing alone. This project brings the track's lessons together in a 1300 kg car:

- **Acceleration** (lessons 1–4): power, gears and **traction**. With lots of power, front-wheel drive spins its tyres — weight shifts to the rear when accelerating. All-wheel drive uses the grip of all four wheels.
- **Top speed** (lesson 11): power against Cd × A, and a top gear that lets the engine get there.
- **Consumption** (lessons 7 and 18): at 100 km/h it depends on **drag and rolling resistance**, not on engine power — a powerful engine doesn't use more if the car is aerodynamic (in this model, with fixed efficiency).
- **Braking** (lessons 5 and 13): enough brake force and **ABS** to use all the grip without locking.

## Energy and braking

At 100 km/h, a 1300 kg car has ½ × 1300 × 27.8² ≈ **502 kJ** to dissipate. The shortest possible distance with μ = 0.9 is:

```
d = v² / (2 μ g) = 27.8² / (2 × 0.9 × 9.81) ≈ 43.7 m
```

## How to approach it

1. Choose the drive and the power for the 0–100.
2. Tune the aerodynamics (top speed **and** consumption improve together).
3. Set the ratios so the engine reaches top speed.
4. Brakes: force and ABS.

Then run it and see which goals are still missing — engineering is iteration.
car-20-projeto-esportivo.task: Design the sports car: **0–100 km/h within 6.5 s** without wheelspin (**up to 0.5 s** of spin), **top speed ≥ 230 km/h**, **consumption ≤ 5.2 L/100 km** at 100 km/h and **braking from 100 km/h within 46 m**.
hints: With front-wheel drive the car spins and can't get below ~8 s, even with more power. Try all-wheel drive with ~150 kW.
Cd 0.28 and an area of 2.0 m² take care of consumption and top speed; final drive near 3.6. A 12 kN brake with ABS on.
goals: Top speed of at least 230 km/h
Consumption up to 5.2 L/100 km at 100 km/h

questions.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a **1300 kg** car at **100 km/h**? Answer in kJ.
What is the shortest possible braking distance from **100 km/h** with μ = **0.9**? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.explanation: d = 27.78² / (2 × 0.9 × 9.81) ≈ 43.7 m. With ABS (95% of the limit) the car gets close to it.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't simply adding power to a **front-wheel-drive** car improve its 0–100?
options: Because the gearbox can't take it
Because when accelerating the weight shifts back and the front wheels spin: grip is the limit
questions.explanation: The maximum force at the wheels is μ × load on the driven axle; under acceleration load leaves the front. AWD uses all four wheels.
